title: Full Walkthrough: Workflow for AI Coding — Matt Pocock
summary: Matt Pocock workshop: grill-me alignment, PRD, vertical-slice Kanban issues, AFK Ralph loops with TDD and deep modules.

assertions.quote: as you continually keep adding stuff to the same context window, it just gets dumber and dumber

verdicts.note: Long-context benchmarks (e.g. NoLiMa, context-rot studies) show degradation as context grows; the exact threshold is model-dependent.

Vibe-coding MLR (47 sources): context-window/state-retention failures and context drift over long multi-turn sessions are reported, but only by 2 sources and labeled 'emerging'; no 'smart zone' sizing evidence.

assertions.quote: devs love compacting for some reason, but I hate it

verdicts.note: Fresh context avoids accumulated noise, but compaction is useful when state is hard to reconstruct; it is a tradeoff, not a rule.

assertions.quote: I tried this. I really tried it. And it sucks.

verdicts.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

The review recommends reviewing generated code before committing rather than integrating unread output, and warns that deferred understanding (cognitive debt) raises later maintenance costs; this is recommendation-level evidence.

The authors warn that a loss of understanding may hurt review, debugging and maintenance. They also concede that future workflows handing those jobs to agents might make low-level comprehension matter less. So the paper backs the concern only speculatively.

Across 177 open-source projects, the share of merged pull requests that got no code review was the strongest predictor of how much more corrective maintenance agentic code needed than human code (about 6% more burden per 10 percentage points of no-review rate, HR multiplier 1.75, CI 1.01-3.04); an observational, project-level association with a weak overall fit (R2 6%), and it measures merging without review, not a spec-driven workflow that ignores the code.

assertions.quote: Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan

verdicts.note: Requirements clarification before implementation is well-established practice and widely reported to reduce agent rework.
Tracer-bullet/vertical slicing gives earlier integration feedback; applies to agents as to humans.

assertions.quote: the quality of your feedback loops influences how good your AI can code

verdicts.note: Agent benchmarks and practice consistently show verifiable feedback (tests, compilers) is the main driver of agent success.

assertions.quote: TDD I found is absolutely essential for getting the most out of agents

verdicts.note: Tests-first gives agents a target and limits test-cheating; evidence is mostly anecdotal and it does not suit all code (e.g. UI).

assertions.quote: bad code bases make bad agents

verdicts.note: Clear module boundaries help both humans and agents navigate and test; consistent with Ousterhout and practitioner reports.

assertions.quote: planning, this alignment phase, has to be human in the loop

verdicts.note: Current agents are weakest at intent/requirements and strongest at well-specified implementation with verification.

Anthropic: most staff can 'fully delegate' only 0-20% of their work and actively supervise the rest, keeping design for themselves; this supports keeping a human on design but shows implementation is also rarely left unattended.

assertions.quote: the reviewer will be dumber than the thing that actually implemented it

verdicts.note: Fresh-context reviewers avoid self-confirmation and context bloat; plausible and commonly practiced but little hard evidence.
Agents treat repo docs as authoritative; outdated docs demonstrably steer them wrong.

assertions.quote: I think we just need to be ready to be doing more code review

verdicts.note: Surveys and studies (e.g. Faros, Google) report increased PR volume and review load with AI adoption.
The review finds developer work shifts from writing code toward specification, supervision and validation, with the unit of work moving to the acceptance decision.

METR 2025 screen recordings (74 issues): with AI, developers spend less time coding and searching and more time reviewing AI output, prompting and waiting; supports a shift toward review, though QA/testing time is not singled out.
Anthropic interviews: engineers describe becoming 'managers of AI agents', and one estimated their work shifted '70%+ to being a code reviewer/reviser'; this is qualitative self-report.

assertions.quote: software engineering fundamentals ... also works super well with AI

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.

assertions.quote: Should I be reviewing this document? ... I don't look at these

verdicts.note: Reviewing plans catches costly mistakes early (e.g. editing secrets), but some practitioners get similar alignment through interactive Q&A and skip reading plans; value depends on task risk.

assertions.quote: you need to own as much of your planning stack as you possibly can

verdicts.note: Owning and understanding your workflow helps you debug it, and many practitioners report framework bloat; but there is no comparative evidence, and frameworks can be a good starting point.

Google built its own pipeline of reusable steps and deliberately chose agentless techniques over complex planning agents, citing Agentless results and cost, which supports simple self-built workflows for migrations.

assertions.quote: implementation here is really the only AFK bit

verdicts.note: Goal/loop features keep agents going through backlogs, but unattended runs drift or game checks without good verification; works when acceptance tests are strong.

Airbnb's custom loop runner re-prompted the LLM with errors until a step passed or a retry cap was hit, and the first bulk run migrated 75% of 3.5K files in 4 hours; this is a bespoke pipeline, not a generic agent goal command.

In AIDev's PRs from popular repositories (over 500 stars), autonomous agents that take a task and open a pull request on their own had 35% (GitHub Copilot), 49% (Devin) and 64% (OpenAI Codex) of their PRs merged, 15 to 40 points below human PRs and lowest on features, bug fixes and performance; the agents do produce work without step-by-step prompting, but every change still went through human review and a third to two thirds were not merged.
